question: Practical guide to help observer organizations, especially first-timers, take part in COP 24 (Katowice, Dec 2018). It did not set out to measure anything.

definitions.definition: Organizations with observer status. There are three categories: UN system and specialized agencies, IGOs, and NGOs. IGOs and NGOs are reviewed before the COP admits them.
definitions.quote: Organizations with observer status are called Observer Organizations. There are three categories of observer organizations - a) United Nations System and its Specialized Agencies b) intergovernmental organizations (IGOs) and c) non-governmental organizations (NGOs).

definitions.definition: Self-organized loose groups of NGOs that mirror the 9 Major Groups. Membership is neither official nor binding.
definitions.quote: They are self-organized loose groups of NGOs with diverse but broadly clustered interests

definitions.definition: Business and industry NGOs, one of the UNFCCC constituencies.
Faith Based Organizations, ECONGO and Parliamentarians have been recognized informally since 2016. They do not have all the privileges of an official constituency.
definitions.quote: These informal NGO groups do not enjoy all privileges of an official constituency.

definitions.definition: Parties, UN and related bodies, media and non-profit observer organizations with observer status may attend. Everyone entering must have a badge.
definitions.quote: Parties to the Convention, United Nations and related organizations and agencies, media and non-profit observer organizations with observer status may attend the sessions of the Convention.

findings.claim: The COP decides on admitting new observer organizations as a standing agenda item, usually on day one.
findings.quote: One of the standing agenda items is the admission of new observer organizations. The COP usually takes a decision on this item at the first day of the conference.

findings.claim: Observer access to closed informal meetings is limited.
findings.quote: Open unless one-third of Parties present at the session object, and the presiding officer may determine at any time to close.

findings.claim: Constituency membership brings benefits such as plenary floor access, office space and bilateral meetings with officials.
findings.quote: access to bilateral meetings with officials; tickets for limited access meetings.

findings.claim: Observers are expected to engage through bilaterals with government delegates to advocate policy perspectives.
findings.quote: Holding bilaterals with government delegates to share position papers and submissions, and advocate policy perspectives.

findings.claim: The guide says UN meetings aim to be open, transparent and inclusive, and participants must follow a code of conduct. The excerpt gives no conflict-of-interest or undue-influence rule.
findings.quote: UN meetings operate on the principles of being open, transparent and inclusive

findings.claim: The list of participants is published as an information document (INF).
findings.quote: Information document Practical data (e.g. list of participants), workshop reports, background documents English INF

limitations.point: The guide covers observers, not Party delegations or Party overflow badges. It has no counts, sector classification, fossil-link definition, or conflict-of-interest or lobbying rules. The only code-of-conduct material is links to harassment, recording and security guidelines, and the guidelines were not in the text.
The text is flattened from a visual layout, so table and constituency structure is partly garbled. Some constituency rows (e.g. the full list of focal points) may be missing.
